concept.name: Error Handling with Result Types

relationships.description: Connects Error Handling with Result Types to jvm internals and garbage collection in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Result types represent the outcome of a fallible operation as an explicit discriminated union (Ok(T) | Err(E)) in the function's return signature rather than throwing out-of-band exceptions.
spark.keyTakeaway: By forcing callers to unwrap or propagate errors at compile time, Result types turn hidden control-flow jumps into type-checked data pipelines with zero stack-unwinding overhead.

concept.whyItMatters: Unchecked exceptions create invisible exit paths in functions: a caller cannot tell from a signature like `chargeCard(orderId): Receipt` whether the function can fail on network timeouts, insufficient funds, or invalid currency. In high-throughput services (e.g., 50k+ RPS payment gateways or parsers), throwing and capturing stack traces costs 1–10 microseconds per exception and breaks linear composition. Result types make failure modes part of the API contract, enabling exhaustive pattern matching, railway-oriented chaining (`map`, `andThen`), and predictable latency.
whenToUse: Expected domain and I/O failures such as validation errors, HTTP 4xx/5xx responses, rate limits, or record-not-found lookups where the caller must decide how to recover.
Performance-critical hot paths (parsers, codecs, network proxies, trading engines) where JVM/CLR stack-trace allocation on error paths causes tail-latency spikes.
Functional and concurrent pipelines (Java CompletableFuture/sealed interfaces, Rust Result<T, E>, TypeScript neverthrow) where errors must travel cleanly across async boundaries or thread pools.
whenNotToUse: Truly unrecoverable programmer bugs or invariant violations (null-pointer dereference, out-of-bounds array index, OOM, corrupted heap) that should panic or crash fast.
Deeply nested UI or scripting glue where every intermediate call only logs and aborts, and the host language lacks `?` or `flatMap` ergonomics—causing verbose boilerplate.
Legacy frameworks (Spring MVC `@ControllerAdvice`, JAX-RS mappers) whose entire middleware stack already relies on typed exception interception unless you wrap at the boundary.
keyPoints: Explicit signatures: `Result<PaymentReceipt, PaymentError>` documents both the happy path and the finite set of domain errors in the type system.
Exhaustive handling: sealed interfaces (Java 21+), Rust `enum`, or TypeScript discriminated unions force callers to handle every error variant or explicitly propagate it.
Monadic composition: `map` transforms `Ok` values without touching `Err`, while `flatMap` (`andThen`) short-circuits a chain of fallible steps on the first `Err`.
Zero-cost error paths: returning an `Err` struct allocates a small value on the stack or heap without walking and symbolizing 40+ stack frames.
Boundary translation: convert low-level exceptions (JDBC `SQLException`, `IOException`) into typed domain `Result` variants at repository or client boundaries.

examples.title: Stripe-Style Payment Capture Pipeline in Java 21
examples.scenario: A checkout service validates a cart, reserves inventory in Redis, and captures funds via an external PSP. Previously, `PaymentException` was caught three layers up, masking whether a failure was retryable (HTTP 503) or terminal (card declined).
examples.outcome: Modeling the return type as `sealed interface CaptureResult permits Captured, Declined, TransientGatewayFailure` lets the orchestrator pattern-match exhaustively: `TransientGatewayFailure` schedules an exponential-backoff retry in Kafka, while `Declined` immediately surfaces a 402 to the client—cutting misclassified retries by 94%.

examples.title: High-Throughput Log Parser in Rust / Python
examples.scenario: An ingestion worker parses 120,000 JSON/Syslog lines per second. Roughly 3% of incoming lines are malformed; raising `ValueError` in Python or `Exception` in Java spent 38% of CPU time building stack frames.
examples.outcome: Returning `Result<ParsedEvent, ParseError>` (a 16-byte tagged struct with line offset and error enum) eliminated stack-trace allocation, dropping p99 batch parse latency from 42 ms to 11 ms and routing `Err` payloads directly to a dead-letter topic.

tradeOffs.pro: Every possible failure is visible at the call site, preventing silent swallowed errors or surprise runtime crashes.
tradeOffs.con: In languages without `?` propagation syntax (like Java or Go without generics sugar), chaining 5+ fallible calls requires verbose `flatMap` lambdas or repetitive `if (res.isErr())` checks.

tradeOffs.pro: Avoids `Throwable.fillInStackTrace()`, making error paths 10x–100x faster under high error rates (e.g., bot traffic or malformed input bursts).
tradeOffs.con: Every happy-path return wraps the value in a `Result` container (unless stack-allocated or value-typed), adding a minor wrapper allocation in GC languages.

tradeOffs.pro: Structured error enums carry domain fields (`retryAfterMs`, `fieldName`, `upstreamCode`) that serialize cleanly to JSON logs and metrics.
tradeOffs.con: Lacks an automatic call-stack trace by default; engineers must attach explicit context frames (`wrapErr("loading user 42")`) or correlation IDs when propagating across layers.

failureModes.name: Result-Wrapping Without Context (Context Loss)
failureModes.description: Propagating a bare `Err(NotFound)` up six service layers makes logs useless because you cannot tell whether the missing record was a User, Merchant, or PromoCode.
failureModes.mitigation: Attach contextual error wrappers at layer boundaries (`mapErr(e -> new OrderLoadError(orderId, e))`) and include a structured `traceId`.

failureModes.name: Panic via Unchecked `.unwrap()` in Production
failureModes.description: Developers bypass the type safety of `Result` by calling `.unwrap()` or `.get()` on happy-path assumptions, turning recoverable errors into process crashes.
failureModes.mitigation: Ban `.unwrap()` in production code via linter rules (Clippy `unwrap_used`, ArchUnit/ErrorProne) and allow only `.unwrapOr()`, `.match()`, or explicit propagation.

failureModes.name: Stringly-Typed `Result<T, String>`
failureModes.description: Using `String` as the error type `E` forces callers to parse English error messages with regexes to decide between retrying and failing fast.
failureModes.mitigation: Restrict `E` to a closed `enum` or `sealed interface` where each variant encodes machine-actionable metadata.

failureModes.name: Leaky Infrastructure Errors in Domain Signatures
failureModes.description: Returning `Result<Order, SQLException>` from a business service couples callers to PostgreSQL internals and breaks abstraction boundaries.
failureModes.mitigation: Map `SQLException` SQLState codes (e.g., `23505` unique violation) into domain errors (`DuplicateOrder`, `StorageUnavailable`) inside the repository adapter.

commonMistakes: Mixing exceptions and Result types in the same method so callers must catch `Throwable` AND unwrap a `Result`.
Using `Result<Void, Error>` for operations that cannot fail instead of returning `void` or `Unit`.
Dropping the original cause when mapping `Err(lowLevel)` to `Err(highLevel)`, breaking root-cause diagnostics.
Ignoring returned `Result` values on side-effecting calls like `auditLog.write()`—always enforce `@CheckReturnValue` or `#[must_use]`.
Putting stack traces inside every `Err` object by default, which reintroduces the exact allocation overhead Result types were meant to avoid.

sections.content:
## The idea

Exceptions implement non-local `goto`: when a function throws, the runtime suspends normal execution, unwinds stack frames until it finds a matching `catch` block, and allocates a stack trace along the way. Because `throws` clauses are often unchecked (Python, TypeScript, Go `panic`, Java `RuntimeException`), callers have no compile-time guarantee that they handled failure modes.

Result types invert this model by treating failure as ordinary data. A function that can fail returns a tagged union `Result<T, E>` with exactly two mutually exclusive states: `Ok(T)` holding the success payload, or `Err(E)` holding a typed error value. Because `Result<T, E>` is not `T`, the compiler refuses to let you read the `T` without first inspecting the tag—either via pattern matching, `map`/`flatMap` combinators, or early-return propagation.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an order-fulfillment step `reserveAndCharge(OrderRequest req)` that must: (1) validate SKU quantities, (2) reserve stock in Redis via a Lua script, and (3) charge the customer's card via Stripe. Using railway-oriented programming, each step returns `Result<StepOutput, CheckoutError>`:

1. `validate(req)` returns `Ok(ValidatedOrder)` or short-circuits with `Err(InvalidQuantity(sku))`.
2. `reserveStock(order)` runs only if step 1 returned `Ok`. If Redis reports insufficient inventory, it returns `Err(OutOfStock(sku, available=0))`—skipping the Stripe call entirely.
3. `chargeCard(reservation)` runs only if step 2 returned `Ok`. If Stripe returns HTTP 402, it returns `Err(CardDeclined(reason))`, and a compensating `onErr` hook releases the Redis reservation.
4. At the HTTP controller boundary, a single exhaustive `switch` maps `Ok(receipt)` -> HTTP 200, `InvalidQuantity` -> HTTP 400, `OutOfStock` -> HTTP 409, and `CardDeclined` -> HTTP 402.

sections.content:
## Language mechanics and ergonomics

How cleanly Result types work depends heavily on language support for algebraic data types (ADTs) and propagation syntax:

- **Rust (`std::result::Result<T, E>`)**: Built into the standard library with `#[must_use]`. The `?` operator unwraps `Ok(v)` or returns `Err(From::from(e))` in a single character, giving exception-like brevity with compile-time checking.
- **Java 21+ (Sealed Interfaces + Pattern Matching)**: While `java.util` lacks a built-in `Result`, a 15-line `sealed interface Result<T, E> permits Ok, Err` combined with `switch (res) { case Ok(var v) -> ...; case Err(var e) -> ...; }` gives full exhaustiveness checking without third-party dependencies (or use Vavr `Either`/`Try`).
- **Python 3.10+ (`returns` library or `@dataclass` unions)**: Typing `Result = Ok[T] | Err[E]` with `match res:` (PEP 634) enables static checking via `mypy --strict` or `pyright`, though runtime overhead remains higher than native Rust enums.

## Comparing error-handling models

| Mechanism | Compile-Time Exhaustiveness | Error-Path Cost | Control Flow Visibility | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Result Types (`Result<T, E>`)** | Yes (with sealed/enum `E`) | ~1–10 ns (no stack walk) | Explicit in return type | Domain logic, parsers, distributed I/O |
| **Unchecked Exceptions** | No (hidden from signature) | 1–10 µs (`fillInStackTrace`) | Invisible jump to `catch` | Unexpected bugs, framework middleware |
| **Checked Exceptions (Java)** | Partial (breaks lambdas/Streams) | 1–10 µs (`fillInStackTrace`) | Explicit via `throws` | Legacy Java APIs without functional chains |
| **Go `(T, error)` Tuple** | No (`nil, nil` is possible) | ~1–5 ns (interface boxing) | Explicit but manual `if err != nil` | Simple procedural services with shallow stacks |
| **Error Codes (`errno` / `int`)** | No (easy to ignore) | <1 ns | Implicit global or int return | C/kernel syscalls and FFI boundaries |

## Failure modes

- **Silent Discarding**: If the language does not warn on unused return values, calling `sendEmail()` and ignoring its `Result` silently drops failures. Enforce `@CheckReturnValue` (Java ErrorProne) or `#[must_use]` (Rust).
- **Error-Type Explosion**: Defining a single giant `AppError` enum with 80 variants forces unrelated modules to depend on every error in the system. Instead, scope error unions per module (`AuthError`, `BillingError`) and compose at boundaries.
- **Async Wrapper Friction**: Nesting `CompletableFuture<Result<T, E>>` or `Promise<Result<T, E>>` creates awkward double-wrapping (`thenCompose` + `flatMap`). Use a dedicated `AsyncResult<T, E>` helper or structured concurrency.

## Boundary design: Exceptions vs. Results

Production systems rarely use Result types for 100% of code; they draw a crisp boundary between **panics/exceptions** (bugs) and **Results** (expected operational failures):

1. **Inner Core (Domain & Adapters)**: Wrap third-party SDKs (JDBC, AWS SDK, HTTP clients) in thin adapters that catch `IOException`, `TimeoutException`, or `SQLException` and translate them into `Result<T, DomainError>`.
2. **Panic/Defect Boundary**: Let `NullPointerException`, `IllegalStateException` (broken internal invariant), or `OutOfMemoryError` bubble up to a top-level supervisor or HTTP 500 handler that logs the full stack trace and alerts on-call.
3. **Observability**: Emit a structured counter metric `operation_result_total{op="capture", status="err", code="card_declined"}` inside your `Result` constructor or boundary mapper so every error variant is automatically graphed.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Define a closed `sealed interface` or `enum` for every module's error type `E`—never use `String` or raw `Exception`.
- [ ] Enable compiler/linter enforcement (`#[must_use]`, `@CheckReturnValue`, `mypy --strict`) so `Result` values cannot be silently ignored.
- [ ] Ban `.unwrap()` / `.get()` in production paths outside unit tests and startup config parsing.
- [ ] Convert external SDK exceptions into typed `Result` variants at the outermost adapter layer.
- [ ] Attach correlation IDs and contextual operation names when wrapping lower-level `Err` values upward.
- [ ] Keep unrecoverable programmer bugs (invariant violations, OOM) on the panic/exception path with full stack traces.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Error Handling Result Types

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Result types represent the outcome of a fallible operation as an explicit discriminated union (Ok(T) | Err(E)) in the function's return signature rather than throwing out-of-band exceptions.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: reserveStock() applies the primary invariant and coordinates with chargeCard().

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, chargeCard() experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Attach contextual error wrappers at layer boundaries (`mapErr(e -> new OrderLoadError(orderId, e))`) and include a structured `traceId`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: By forcing callers to unwrap or propagate errors at compile time, Result types turn hidden control-flow jumps into type-checked data pipelines with zero stack-unwinding overhead.
Avoid trap: Mixing exceptions and Result types in the same method so callers must catch `Throwable` AND unwrap a `Result`.
Avoid trap: Using `Result<Void, Error>` for operations that cannot fail instead of returning `void` or `Unit`.
When to reach for it: Expected domain and I/O failures such as validation errors, HTTP 4xx/5xx responses, rate limits, or record-not-found lookups where the caller must decide how to recover.
When to reach for it: Performance-critical hot paths (parsers, codecs, network proxies, trading engines) where JVM/CLR stack-trace allocation on error paths causes tail-latency spikes.

putItTogether.title: Putting Error Handling Result Types Together
putItTogether.summary: By forcing callers to unwrap or propagate errors at compile time, Result types turn hidden control-flow jumps into type-checked data pipelines with zero stack-unwinding overhead.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Error Handling Result Types before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Modeling the return type as `sealed interface CaptureResult permits Captured, Declined, TransientGatewayFailure` lets the orchestrator pattern-match exhaustively: `TransientGatewayFailure` schedules an exponential-backoff retry in Kafka, while `Declined` immediately surfaces a 402 to the client—cutting misclassified retries by 94%.
